lines.text: Take one small feature. A person can claim a name.
To ship it, you write that same fact over and over. A route. A validator. An SDK method. A CLI command. A tool for agents. A page of docs.
Six copies of one idea, kept in sync by hand.
Change one, and the others quietly go stale.
Orthograph starts somewhere else.
Describe a system once, and everything else falls out of it.
Here's the whole idea on one sheet.
On the left is what you write: the blueprint. Small, typed declarations of what your system is.
Orthograph compiles them into one model.
From that model, it generates the server, the HTTP API, the SDK, the command line tool, the MCP tools, the docs, and more.
The only code you write by hand is behaviour: one handler per operation.
And you don't just claim it works. Stories run against the real system, and the result is a verdict.
Let's take one feature all the way through.
Our app is called Plugged In. You claim a name, and you get a public page of links.
Start with a thing. A handle has an id, a name, and an owner.
Next, its machine: the states a handle can be in, and the moves between them. Claimed, then released.
Now the verb. Claim is an operation on a handle.
It says what comes in, what goes back, and which move it makes.
Who may call it, and what it's allowed to write.
That the same request twice counts once, and how fast it has to be.
Last, the rules. A name has one holder. A person holds one name. Each rule owns its own refusal.
That's the whole description. Notice what isn't here: no route, no request parsing, no command line flags.
Run ortho check.
It compiles the blueprint, and it refuses a description that doesn't hold together.
What comes out is the model: one JSON file, with every declaration in it, each one hashed.
Everything after this is made from the model, never from your files directly.
Now, ortho generate.
From those ten lines, you get an HTTP endpoint, with its payload, answer, and refusals all typed.
An SDK function.
A command in your app's own command line tool.
An MCP tool, so any agent can call it. It's already described, including how it refuses.
A docs page, with every refusal and its code.
And the served operation itself, next to the portal and the infrastructure plan.
Each of these is a projection: one view of the same model, made by code.
They're never yours to edit. Change one by hand, and the check fails.
Here's the rule that holds it all together. Each operation is enforced in exactly one place.
Every way in reaches that one place. HTTP, the SDK, the command line, an agent's tool. None of them decides anything on its own.
So when Bob tries to claim a name that's taken, the refusal is the same everywhere. Same name. Same code.
So what's left for you to write? Behaviour.
Orthograph scaffolds one handler per operation, once. From then on it's yours, and it's never overwritten.
The header lists everything the runtime already does, so your code doesn't.
The body is ordinary TypeScript, written with Effect. Save the handle and its page. Make the move. Answer.
It never checks who's calling. It never parses a request. It never refuses a taken name. The declaration already said all of that.
How do you know it works? A journey.
A journey is a story told through real operations. A different agent from the builder writes it, before the handler exists.
Aaron claims a free name. Expect an id back. Expect the event. Expect the handle to be in the state claimed. And expect these spans in the trace.
ortho prove starts a real world, with real stores, runs every story, and judges what they left behind.
With an empty handler, it's red, and it tells you exactly where.
So building is climbing. Fix the handler, prove again, and repeat until every journey is green. A coding agent can run that loop by itself.
Seven journeys. Fifty-six steps. Nine evals on every operation. Done is a verdict, not a claim.
Now change something. Tighten claim's budget, and reword its description.
The check notices right away: eight generated files no longer match the model.
Generate, and they're remade. The SDK, the command line, the MCP tool, the docs.
Then ortho impact tells you what the change made stale. Only claim. Everything else is still proven.
Prove again, and you're green.
That's the loop. Describe. Compile. Generate. Write the behaviour. Prove. Then ship it, and watch it run.
What flows down is the description. What flows back is evidence.
You write the blueprint, the handlers, and the journeys.
You get the server, the API, the SDK, the command line, the agent tools, and the docs.
And you know it works, because it's proved.
Orthograph. Describe a system once, and everything else falls out of it.
